correctness.rationale: Exact convolution kernel equals exp(-2t) I_abs(n)(2t). Riccati equation for I_n prime/I_n proves strict order in n and a unique crossing at x_n>n^2, excluding tangencies. Sign ordering and telescoping yield the sharp endpoint norm and all sign-extremizers. Uniform local Fourier/Edgeworth expansions with differentiated error bounds give x_n=n^2+1/2+O(n^-2) and an adjacent-kernel expansion whose second coefficient is 1/6 minus the squared rounding displacement; after x=2t the coefficient is 1/12-rho^2/2. Rounding boundaries differ O(1) in x, implying uniform O(t^-3/2) relative remainder. The checker runs 134 finite tests but infinite statements are proved analytically.

originality.rationale: The examined classical and contemporary heat-kernel references give modified-Bessel representations and qualitative or order-sharp difference estimates, but no exact all-time endpoint norm with uniquely ordered sign-change thresholds or oscillatory second-order coefficient. The scalar Bessel threshold system and lattice-phase accumulation interval are distinct positive claims. This is a best-knowledge priority assessment, not proof that no historical equivalent exists.
residual_risks: An equivalent exact norm/phase law may have appeared under Skellam signed total variation, Bessel derivative-ratio, or discrete semigroup smoothing terminology outside the retrieved historical sources.
Although the closest 2021 theorem was compared at full-text level, a literature search cannot establish worldwide priority or substitute independent mathematical assessment.

value.rationale: Exact sharp endpoint time-smoothing norms are natural operator-theoretic stability quantities for discrete diffusion. The theorem gives an all-time computable closed Bessel extremum, exact spatial sign structure and maximizer switches, a sharp leading continuum rate, and a nonconvergent next-order coefficient with a full interval of limit points. These are structurally meaningful, not an arbitrary isolated parameter or routine repackaging of the kernel formula.
